log-square.title: Polynomial versus log
log-square.prompt: For f=n and g=(log n)², what is the relation?
log-square.hint: Any positive power of n outruns a fixed log power.

help.concept: The ratio n/(log n)² tends to infinity.

nlog-over-log.prompt: For f=n log n+n and g=log n, what is the relation?

worked-limits-one-eight.title: Worked Limit Comparisons: Constants, Polynomials, and Logs
worked-limits-one-eight.bodyMarkdown:
Apply the ratio rule to the first eight pairs from the handout.

1. `2 / 5 → 2/5`, so `2 = Θ(5)`.
2. `(5n) / 7 → ∞`, so `5n = Ω(7)`.
3. `(3n²) / n² → 3`, so `3n² = Θ(n²)`.
4. `(3n² + 7n) / (2n²) = 3/2 + 7/(2n) → 3/2`, so the pair is `Θ`.
5. `(2n⁴ - 3n² + 7) / n⁵ = 2/n - 3/n³ + 7/n⁵ → 0`, so `f = O(g)`.
6. `log(n²) / (log n + 5) = 2log n / (log n + 5) → 2`, so `f = Θ(g)`.
7. `n / (log n)² → ∞`. Applying L’Hôpital twice produces `n/(2log n)` and then `n/2`, so `f = Ω(g)`.
8. `(n log n + n) / log n = n + n/log n → ∞`, so `f = Ω(g)`.

### What to notice

- Equal highest powers leave a positive constant.
- A lower-degree numerator over a higher-degree denominator tends to zero.
- Every positive power of `n` eventually outgrows every fixed power of `log n`.
- Changing the base of a logarithm multiplies by a constant and does not change a `Θ` class.

polynomial-log-animation.title: Cancel, Normalize, or Differentiate
polynomial-log-animation.context: Choose the algebraic move that exposes the dominant growth.

steps.title: Cancel matching highest powers
steps.body: When numerator and denominator have degree 2, divide every term by n².

steps.title: Higher denominator degree wins
steps.body: After dividing by n⁵, every term contains a negative power of n.

steps.title: A power of n outruns log powers
steps.body: Repeated L’Hôpital differentiation eventually exposes a linear term that diverges.
